No peeking!

2. How do you store the value `150` in a variable called `x`?

  - `1gene`
  - `cell count`
  - `gene_A`
  - `Gene_A`

---

::: {.section-tag}
🔁 Review: Lecture 5
:::

### ✅ Rapid Fire 1 — Syntax & Variables

1. Nothing crashes and **nothing runs**. The console sits on a **`+`** prompt, waiting for the rest of the string — it stays stuck until every quote and bracket matches
2. **`x <- 150`**
3. `1gene` and `cell count` → **syntax errors, R stops**. `Gene_A` → **legal but dangerous**: a different variable from `gene_A`. `gene_A` → **safe**

---

::: {.section-tag}
🔁 Review: Lecture 5
:::

### ⚡ Rapid Fire 2 — Types, Math & Strings

::: {.slide-kicker}
No peeking!
:::

1. What type is `150`? What type is `"EGFR"`?
2. `10 %% 3` versus `10 %/% 3`?
3. `read.csv("data\visium\counts.csv")` crashes. Why, and what is the rule?

---

::: {.section-tag}
🔁 Review: Lecture 5
:::

### ✅ Rapid Fire 2 — Types, Math & Strings

1. `150` is **`numeric`**. `"EGFR"` is **`character`** — the quotes make it text, so it can never be counted or averaged
2. `1` and `3`: **`%%`** returns the remainder, **`%/%`** floor-divides
3. `\` is the **escape character**, so `\v` and `\c` are invalid codes. The rule: **always use forward slashes `/`** in R paths

---

::: {.section-tag}
🔁 Review: Lecture 5
:::

### ⚡ Rapid Fire 3 — Operators & Control Flow

::: {.slide-kicker}
No peeking!
:::

1. Your `if` tested one condition and it came back `FALSE`. How do you check a **second** condition?
2. Write the R test for `500 <= x <= 2500`.
3. In a `for` loop, how do `next` and `break` differ?

---

::: {.section-tag}
🔁 Review: Lecture 5
:::

### ✅ Rapid Fire 3 — Operators & Control Flow

1. Add an **`else if`** — it runs only when the condition above it was `FALSE`, and the **first** `TRUE` branch wins
2. Two comparisons joined: **`(x >= 500) & (x <= 2500)`**. R has no chained comparisons
3. `next` **skips** the rest of the current iteration and keeps going; `break` **aborts the loop entirely**

## 📂 The Question

Which genes change when apatinib hits **resistant** cells — and do the *same* genes change in the **sensitive** ones?


- **To analyze, we need:** a **count matrix** (39,376 genes × 12 samples)

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🎯 Today Is Plumbing
The whole lecture is about getting this one object into R **correctly** — structures, strings, `NA`, `apply`, functions, merging. 
:::

## 📂 Before We Download

Let's make a folder for the data.

```bash
mkdir -p counts      # create it once
cd counts
```

---

## 📂 curl: Fetch the Counts Matrix

```bash
curl -o counts.tsv.gz \
  "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?type=rnaseq_counts&acc=GSE129221&format=file&file=GSE129221_raw_counts_GRCh38.p13_NCBI.tsv.gz"

gunzip counts.tsv.gz     # .tsv.gz -> .tsv
```


::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Always `-o`, Always Quote
GEO's `content-disposition` header makes `-O` unreliable here, so name the file yourself.
:::

---

## 📂 Why a Script?

That was two lines — and one was a **136-character URL**.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**By hand**

* a mistyped character
* a different file tomorrow
* thirty files next week
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**By script**

* `./download.sh`
* edit one line
* same result, every time
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
### ♻️ Six Months From Now
A script is a text file anyone can read. A shell history is not.
:::

---

## 📂 download.sh

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

OUT_DIR="./counts"
mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR"

curl -o "$OUT_DIR/counts.tsv.gz" \
  "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?type=rnaseq_counts&acc=GSE129221&format=file&file=GSE129221_raw_counts_GRCh38.p13_NCBI.tsv.gz"

gunzip -f "$OUT_DIR/counts.tsv.gz"

echo "File downloaded at $OUT_DIR/counts.tsv:"
ls -lh "$OUT_DIR"

echo "Head of the file:"
head -n 5 "$OUT_DIR/counts.tsv"
```

::: {.callout-note}
### 🧊 `set -euo pipefail` in One Line
Stop on the first error · fail on unset variables · fail on any failed pipe. Without it, a broken download scrolls past and you analyse an HTML error page as counts.
:::

---

## 📂 Making the script executable


```bash
chmod +x download.sh    # RUN ONLY ONCE!
./download.sh           # Script is executable now!
```

## 📋 1. R Data Structures

::: {.agenda data-section="1"}
:::

---

### The Family Tree

![](../_assets/r_data_structures.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.5em; text-align: center; color: #999;"}
Source: [geeksforgeeks.org](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/r-language/data-structures-in-r-programming/)
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### 🎯 What You Will Actually Use
Vectors and data frames every single day. Matrices for count matrices and images. Lists hide behind `read.csv()`, model fits and packages. Factors for every categorical annotation.
:::

---

### Vectors — Same Type, One Dimension

A **vector** is a 1D chain of values that all share the same type.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../_assets/vector.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr-r}
vals <- c(10, 20, 30)
vals
```
:::

::::


---

### Vectors — Same Type, One Dimension


A plain sequence:

```{webr-r}
1:5
```

and a custom one
```{webr-r}
seq(2, 10, by = 2)
```

Or, repetition:

```{webr-r}
rep(1, 10) # repeat 1 ten times
```

::: {.callout-note}
Once a vector exists, every function in R expects one. `mean()`, `sum()`, `length()` all take vectors.
:::


---

### Subsetting Vectors

**Counting Starts at 1**

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
gene_reads <- c(1200, 450, 0, 89, 3300)
gene_reads
```

```{webr-r}
gene_reads[2]     # one value (the 2nd element)
```

```{webr-r}
gene_reads[2:4]   # a range
```

```{webr-r}
gene_reads[-2]    # negative index REMOVES element 2
```

::: {.callout-important}
### 🧬 Bio Example
`gene_reads[gene_reads > 500]` keeps only the highly expressed genes — the R version of filtering a column in Excel. Index `0` does not exist, so the first element is `[1]`, never `[0]`.
:::


---

### Matrices — Same Type, Two Dimensions

A **matrix** is a 2D grid where every cell holds the same type. Spot metadata matrices are exactly this shape.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../_assets/matrix.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.callout-warning}
### ⚠️ Fills by Column
Values fill down columns by default. Add `byrow = TRUE` to fill row-by-row.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
# 3 genes (rows) x 2 cohorts (cols)
count_mat <- matrix(c(120, 45, 0, 310, 85, 12), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
count_mat
```

```{webr-r}
dim(count_mat)      # [rows, cols]
```

```{webr-r}
count_mat[1, 2]     # Row 1 (Gene 1), Col 2 (Cohort 2)
```
:::

::::


---

### Naming Rows and Columns

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
count_mat <- matrix(c(120, 45, 0, 310, 85, 12), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)

# Name the 3 genes (rows) and 2 cohorts (columns)
rownames(count_mat) <- c("EPCAM", "CD3D", "PECAM1")
colnames(count_mat) <- c("Tumor", "Normal")
count_mat
```

```{webr-r}
count_mat[, "Tumor"]     # Entire 'Tumor' column across all genes
```

```{webr-r}
count_mat["EPCAM", ]     # Entire 'EPCAM' row across all cohorts
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Labelled matrices print like a real annotation table — always name them before you show anyone your numbers.
:::


---

### Arrays — Matrices Stacked

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../_assets/array.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.callout-note}
### 🖼️ Bio Example
Arrays are 3D+ data. Histology H&E images (height × width × RGB channels) are stored this way.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
# 2 rows x 3 cols x 2 slices (e.g. RGB / intensity channels)
layers <- array(c(255, 128, 45, 0, 89, 210, 180, 95, 15, 0, 72, 190), 
                dim = c(2, 3, 2))
layers
```

```{webr-r}
dim(layers)       # [rows, cols, slices]
```

```{webr-r}
layers[1, 2, 1]   # Row 1, Col 2, Slice 1
```
:::

::::


---

### Lists — A Box of Anything

Elements can have completely different types and lengths

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../_assets/list.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.callout-important}
### 💡 `[[ ]]` vs `[ ]`
`[[ ]]` extracts the **actual value**. `[ ]` extracts a **sublist** holding the value. Always use `[[ ]]` (or `$`) to compute with the data.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
spot <- list(name = "Visium_S1", 
             counts = c(120, 45, 0), 
             qc_pass = TRUE)
spot
```

```{webr-r}
spot[["qc_pass"]]   # Extracts value
```

```{webr-r}
spot["qc_pass"]     # Extracts a sublist
```
:::

::::


---

### Data Frames — The Workhorse

A **data frame** is a 2D table where each column keeps its own type. This is your spot-metadata table.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../_assets/data_frame.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.callout-note}
### 💡 Columns are Vectors
Each column is a **vector** wearing a name. That is why you can do `spots$umi_count > 10` and get a logical vector back.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
spots <- data.frame(
  spot_id   = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  umi_count = c(12, 45, 0),
  in_tissue = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

spots
```
:::

::::


---

### Getting Oriented in a Data Frame

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
spots <- data.frame(
  spot_id   = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  umi_count = c(12, 45, 0),
  in_tissue = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
head(spots, n = 2)   # First rows
```

```{webr-r}
dim(spots)           # [rows, columns]
```

```{webr-r}
str(spots)           # Structure: types + preview of values
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🧭 The Five-Line Tour
Run `head()`, `dim()`, `str()` on **every** dataset you meet. Ninety seconds here saves an hour of confused errors later.
:::


---

### Subsetting Data Frames

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
spots <- data.frame(
  spot_id   = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  umi_count = c(12, 45, 0),
  in_tissue = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
spots$umi_count                                     # 1. Extract one column as a vector
```

```{webr-r}
spots[spots$umi_count > 10, ]                      # 2. Filter rows by condition
```

```{webr-r}
spots[spots$in_tissue, c("spot_id", "umi_count")]  # 3. Filter rows AND select columns
```

::: {.callout-important}
### 📐 The Comma Means "and"
`df[rows, columns]` — think of it as `df[what rows I want, what columns I want]`. Leave the row part empty (`df[, 1]`) for "all rows"; leave the column part empty (`df[1, ]`) for "all columns".
:::

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Extra
:::

### Factors — Categories, With an Order

A **factor** stores category labels plus the list of allowed levels — the R way to hold annotation columns.

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
cell_types <- factor(c("T-cell", "B-cell", "T-cell", "T-cell"))
levels(cell_types)
```

```{webr-r}
table(cell_types)
```

::: {.callout-note}
### 💡 Levels Order
Levels are **alphabetical by default**. Specify order with `factor(x, levels = c(...))` before plotting or modelling.
:::

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Extra
:::

### Tibbles — Modern Data Frames

A **tibble** (`tbl_df`) is an enhanced modern data frame from the *tidyverse*.

* **Better printing**: Previews only the first 10 rows and columns that fit your screen.
* **Safer subsetting**: Never silently drops down to a vector when you select one column with `[ , 1]`.
* **Strict typing**: Never converts strings to factors automatically.

::: {.callout-tip}
### 📦 Tibble vs Data Frame
Base R functions always accept data frames; `tibble` objects are 100% compatible and inherit from `data.frame`.
:::

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Extra
:::

### Creating a Tibble

```{webr-r}
library(tibble)

# Tibbles print dimensions and column types (<chr>, <dbl>) clearly:
my_spots <- tibble(
  spot_id   = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  umi_count = c(12, 45, 0),
  in_tissue = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

my_spots
```

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Exercise
:::

### ✍️ Exercise 6.1: What Kind of Object Should This Table Be?

Four genes, three samples:

| gene_id | S1 | S2 | S3 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| gene_A | 2 | 3 | 1 |
| gene_B | 0 | 45 | 12 |
| gene_C | 310 | 85 | 0 |
| gene_D | 89 | 12 | 640 |

Two data types live here: gene IDs (**text**) and read counts (**numbers**).

* a) Vector
* b) Matrix
* c) Array
* d) List
* e) Data frame

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Exercise
:::

### ✅ Exercise 6.1: What Kind of Object Should This Table Be?

**e) Data frame** — the only structure that is both rectangular *and* lets each column keep its own type.

```r
counts <- data.frame(
  gene_id = c("gene_A", "gene_B", "gene_C", "gene_D"),
  S1 = c(2, 0, 310, 89),
  S2 = c(3, 45, 85, 12),
  S3 = c(1, 12, 0, 640),
  row.names = 1
)
```

| Structure | Why it fails |
|:---|:---|
| a) Vector | One long line. No rows, no columns, no way to ask for "S1". |
| b) Matrix | One type for everything. The `gene_id` column is text. |
| c) Array | Same one-type rule, plus a third dimension this table does not have. |
| d) List | Holds anything, but has no row/column order — `tbl[, 1]` means nothing. |

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Exercise
:::

### ✍️ Exercise 6.2: What Shape Is `counts`?

```r
counts <- data.frame(
  gene_id = c("gene_A", "gene_B", "gene_C", "gene_D"),
  S1 = c(2, 0, 310, 89),
  S2 = c(3, 45, 85, 12),
  S3 = c(1, 12, 0, 640),
  row.names = 1
)
```

What does `dim(counts)` give you?

* a) `3 4`
* b) `4 3`
* c) `1 3`
* d) `4 4`

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Exercise
:::

### ✅ Exercise 6.2: What Shape Is `counts`?

**b) `4 3`**

`dim()` is always **rows, then columns**.

* **Rows = genes**, running down the page
* **Columns = samples**, running across the top

```r
dim(counts)              # 4 3
head(rownames(counts))   # "gene_A" "gene_B" "gene_C" ...
```

::: {.callout-note}
### 🧬 Rows Are the Genes
The gene IDs became **row labels**, not a column — that is what `row.names = 1` did. Without it you would have 4 columns and `4 4`.
:::

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Exercise
:::

### ✍️ Exercise 6.3: Pull One Sample

You want the read counts for `S1` only, as a **vector**.

* a) `counts[1, ]`
* b) `counts$S1`
* c) `counts[S1]`
* d) `counts["S1"]`

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. R Data Structures · Exercise
:::

### ✅ Exercise 6.3: Pull One Sample

**b) `counts$S1`** — `$` pulls the column out by name and hands you the bare values.

```r
counts$S1        # 2 0 310 89 — all 4 genes, that one sample
```

| Option | Why not |
|:---|:---|
| a) `counts[1, ]` | one **gene** (`gene_A`), all 3 samples — the wrong way round |
| c) `counts[S1]` | `Error: object 'S1' not found` |
| d) `counts["S1"]` | a **4×1 data frame** — one column, wrapped in a table, not a vector |

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🧬 Want the Vector? Use `[[ ]]`
`counts[[1]]` and `counts[["S1"]]` both unwrap to the same thing: `2 0 310 89`.
:::

## 📋 2. Reading, Writing & Merging Files

::: {.agenda data-section="2"}
:::
---

### Where Am I?

```r
getwd()                      # print the current working directory
dir()                        # list what is inside it
setwd("~/projects/spatial")  # move to a project folder
```

::: {.callout-important}
### 🧬 Never Hard-Code Absolute Paths
`/Users/phongdinh/...` works on your laptop and on nobody else's — every hard-coded path is a reproducibility bug waiting for a co-author or reviewer.
:::

---

### Paths Are Relative to Where You Stand

One path, two folders. Walk into a subdirectory and the **same** line flips its answer:

```r
f <- "FCWT_2026/lecture-06/counts/counts.tsv"
```

From the repo root:

```r
getwd()          # Spatial_Transcriptomics_Course
file.exists(f)   # TRUE
```

Now step one level deeper — nothing about `f` changes:

```r
setwd("FCWT_2026/lecture-06")
getwd()          # Spatial_Transcriptomics_Course/FCWT_2026/lecture-06
file.exists(f)   # FALSE
```

::: {.callout-important}
### 🧬 The File Did Not Move
`counts/counts.tsv` is right where it was. Only `getwd()` changed — and that is enough to make R look somewhere else entirely.
:::

---

### The Fix: Anchor to the Project Root

`here()` builds the path from the project root, so the answer stops depending on where you stand:

```r
library(here)
f <- here("FCWT_2026", "lecture-06", "counts", "counts.tsv")

file.exists(f)   # TRUE — from the repo root
file.exists(f)   # TRUE — from analysis/code/ too
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 📦 Install with `install.packages("here")`
Inside a script, `here::i_am("analysis/code/demo.R")` pins the root explicitly.
:::

---

### Read: the Real Count Matrix

The file you downloaded in the first half of this lecture. It is tab-separated, so `read.delim()` is the right call:

```r
library(here)
f <- here("FCWT_2026", "lecture-06", "counts", "counts.tsv")

counts <- read.delim(f, row.names = 1)

dim(counts)     # 39376 12
head(counts)    # first 6 genes, all 12 samples
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 Why `row.names = 1` on the Way In
The first column holds Entrez gene IDs. With `row.names = 1` that column becomes the labels you address genes by. Without it you get **13** columns, and the IDs sit there as ordinary data.
:::

---

::: {.section-tag}
2. Reading, Writing & Merging Files · Extra
:::

### Large Files: Skip read.csv()

```r
# Base R is correct but slow on big matrices
slow <- read.csv("visium_counts.csv")

# data.table::fread() is 10-100x faster on the same file
library(data.table)
fast <- fread("visium_counts.csv")

# Spot coordinates
coords <- fread("tissue_positions_list.csv")
```

::: {.callout-note}
### ⚡ Rule of Thumb
Under ~100 MB: `read.csv()` is fine. Above that: `data.table::fread()`. You will meet the threshold the day you load your first gene-by-spot matrix.
:::

---

::: {.section-tag}
2. Reading, Writing & Merging Files · Extra
:::

### Base R Table Readers Compared

All `read.*` functions wrap `read.table()`, but differ in default parameters:

::: {.small}
| Function | `sep` | `header` | `dec` | Use Case |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **`read.delim()`** | `\t` (Tab) | `TRUE` | `.` | **TSV count matrices & annotations** |
| `read.csv()` | `,` (Comma) | `TRUE` | `.` | Standard CSV files (US/UK) |
| `read.table()` | `""` (Space) | `FALSE` | `.` | Space-separated raw tables |
| `read.delim2()` / `csv2()` | `\t` / `;` | `TRUE` | `,` | European decimal comma format |
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### ⚡ Large Datasets (>100 MB)
Base R functions load into memory as standard data frames. For huge single-cell matrices, `data.table::fread()` or `readr::read_tsv()` are significantly faster.
:::

---

### The Problem: Opaque Sample IDs

Look at the column headers of your count matrix:

```r
colnames(counts)
# [1] "GSM3702795" "GSM3702796" "GSM3702797" "GSM3702798" ...
```

- GEO accessions (`GSM...`) tell you **nothing** about the biology.
- Which samples are untreated controls? Which received Apatinib? Which are drug-resistant?
- We need **sample metadata** mapped to these accession IDs.

---

### The Metadata Table — First, on Paper

Before any R: this is the table you need. One row per sample, keyed by the `GSM...` ID.

### ⚡ Step 1 — The Sample IDs

The `GSM...` IDs are already in `counts` — they are its column names.

**How do you get the column names of a data frame in R?**

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
1. `rownames()` gave you the gene IDs, three slides ago. There is a twin function for the samples.
2. You have already met `colnames()` — earlier you **set** names on a matrix. Now ask for them instead of setting them.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 1 — The Sample IDs

```r
colnames(counts)
#  [1] "GSM3702795" "GSM3702796" "GSM3702797" "GSM3702798" "GSM3702799"
#  [6] "GSM3702800" "GSM3702801" "GSM3702802" "GSM3702803" "GSM3702804"
# [11] "GSM3702805" "GSM3702806"
```

`counts` has 12 columns, so you get 12 names — one per sample.

---

### Step 2 — The Cell Line

Column 2.

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

| sample_id  | **cell_line** | treatment | replicate |
|:-----------|:---------------|:----------| ---------- |
| GSM3702795 | **PC9** | Control | 1 |
| GSM3702796 | **PC9** | Control | 2 |
| GSM3702797 | **PC9** | Control | 3 |
| GSM3702798 | **PC9** | Apatinib | 1 |
| GSM3702799 | **PC9** | Apatinib | 2 |
| GSM3702800 | **PC9** | Apatinib | 3 |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

| sample_id  | **cell_line** | treatment | replicate |
|:-----------|:---------------|:----------| ---------- |
| GSM3702801 | **PC9GR** | Control | 1 |
| GSM3702802 | **PC9GR** | Control | 2 |
| GSM3702803 | **PC9GR** | Control | 3 |
| GSM3702804 | **PC9GR** | Apatinib | 1 |
| GSM3702805 | **PC9GR** | Apatinib | 2 |
| GSM3702806 | **PC9GR** | Apatinib | 3 |

:::

:::::

---

### ⚡ Step 2 — The Cell Line

Six PC9, then six PC9GR. You could type all twelve out yourself:

```r
cell_line <- c("PC9", "PC9", "PC9", "PC9", "PC9", "PC9",
               "PC9GR", "PC9GR", "PC9GR", "PC9GR", "PC9GR", "PC9GR")
```

It is correct. It is also exactly the kind of line you will mistype on Friday.

**"Six PC9, then six PC9GR" — can R do that repeating for you?**

---

### 🔧 `rep()` — Repeating a Vector

```r
rep(x, times, each)
```

* **`x`** — the vector to repeat
* **`times`** — repeat the **whole vector** that many times
* **`each`** — repeat **every element** that many times

The last two are not interchangeable:

```r
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 3)
# [1] "A" "B" "A" "B" "A" "B"

rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3)
# [1] "A" "A" "A" "B" "B" "B"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 Same Six Values, Different Order
`times` and `each` both return 6 elements. Only `each` keeps the three `"A"`s **together**.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 2 — The Cell Line

```r
cell_line <- rep(c("PC9", "PC9GR"), each = 6)
#  [1] "PC9"   "PC9"   "PC9"   "PC9"   "PC9"   "PC9"   "PC9GR" "PC9GR"
# [10] "PC9GR" "PC9GR" "PC9GR"
```

`c()` lists the two lines. `rep(..., each = 6)` repeats **each** one six times.

---

### Step 3 — The Treatment

Column 3, and the last one.

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

| sample_id  | cell_line | **treatment** | replicate |
|:-----------|:----------|:---------------| ---------- |
| GSM3702795 | PC9 | **Control** | 1 |
| GSM3702796 | PC9 | **Control** | 2 |
| GSM3702797 | PC9 | **Control** | 3 |
| GSM3702798 | PC9 | **Apatinib** | 1 |
| GSM3702799 | PC9 | **Apatinib** | 2 |
| GSM3702800 | PC9 | **Apatinib** | 3 |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

| sample_id  | cell_line | **treatment** | replicate |
|:-----------|:----------|:---------------| ---------- |
| GSM3702801 | PC9GR | **Control** | 1 |
| GSM3702802 | PC9GR | **Control** | 2 |
| GSM3702803 | PC9GR | **Control** | 3 |
| GSM3702804 | PC9GR | **Apatinib** | 1 |
| GSM3702805 | PC9GR | **Apatinib** | 2 |
| GSM3702806 | PC9GR | **Apatinib** | 3 |

:::

:::::

---

### ⚡ Step 3 — The Treatment

Three samples per block, four blocks:

```r
rep(c("Control", "Apatinib"), times = 2, each = 3)
#  [1] "Control"  "Control"  "Control"  "Apatinib" "Apatinib" "Apatinib"
#  [7] "Control"  "Control"  "Control"  "Apatinib" "Apatinib" "Apatinib"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 `each` First, Then `times`
`each = 3` stretches `"Control"` and `"Apatinib"` into runs of three. Then `times = 2` repeats that whole run — once for PC9, once for PC9GR.
:::

---

### Step 4 — The Replicate

Column 4, and the last one.

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

| sample_id  | cell_line | treatment | **replicate** |
|:-----------|:----------|:----------|:---------------|
| GSM3702795 | PC9 | Control | **1** |
| GSM3702796 | PC9 | Control | **2** |
| GSM3702797 | PC9 | Control | **3** |
| GSM3702798 | PC9 | Apatinib | **1** |
| GSM3702799 | PC9 | Apatinib | **2** |
| GSM3702800 | PC9 | Apatinib | **3** |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

| sample_id  | cell_line | treatment | **replicate** |
|:-----------|:----------|:----------|:---------------|
| GSM3702801 | PC9GR | Control | **1** |
| GSM3702802 | PC9GR | Control | **2** |
| GSM3702803 | PC9GR | Control | **3** |
| GSM3702804 | PC9GR | Apatinib | **1** |
| GSM3702805 | PC9GR | Apatinib | **2** |
| GSM3702806 | PC9GR | Apatinib | **3** |

:::

:::::

---

### ⚡ Step 4 — The Replicate

Inside every group of three, number the samples 1, 2, 3 — then do it four times over:

```r
replicate <- rep(1:3, times = 4)
# [1] 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 Here It Is `times`, Not `each`
Steps 2 and 3 repeated **each** element. This column repeats the **whole** run `1 2 3` — so `each` would be wrong.
:::

---

### From Table to Data Frame — One Column at a Time

Each column is just a vector. Build them separately, then combine:

```r
# 1. the IDs — you already have them
sample_id <- colnames(counts)

# 2. cell line: six PC9, then six PC9GR
cell_line <- rep(c("PC9", "PC9GR"), each = 6)

# 3. treatment: two treatments, three samples each, twice over
treatment <- rep(c("Control", "Apatinib"), times = 2, each = 3)

# 4. replicate: 1, 2, 3 inside each group of three
replicate <- rep(1:3, times = 4)
```

---

### Four Vectors → One Data Frame

Four vectors of length 12 → one data frame:

```r
sample_info <- data.frame(
  sample_id = sample_id,
  cell_line = cell_line,
  treatment = treatment,
  replicate = replicate
)

sample_info
#    sample_id cell_line treatment replicate
#  1 GSM3702795       PC9   Control         1
#  2 GSM3702796       PC9   Control         2
#  3 GSM3702797       PC9   Control         3
#  4 GSM3702798       PC9  Apatinib         1
#  ...
# 12 GSM3702806     PC9GR  Apatinib         3
```

---

### 🔧 `write.csv()` — Saving a Data Frame

```r
write.csv(x, file, row.names = TRUE)
```

* **`x`** — the object to save
* **`file`** — the path, in quotes, ending in `.csv`
* **`row.names`** — keep the row labels? Default `TRUE`

One argument decides whether the file gets a stray leading header cell:

```r
write.csv(mydf, "mydf.csv")                     # "", "sample_id","cell_line",...
write.csv(mydf, "mydf.csv", row.names = FALSE)  #        "sample_id","cell_line",...
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 `row.names` Depends on What the Labels Mean
Row labels that *mean* something — gene IDs — keep them. Automatic `1..12` row numbers carry nothing, so drop them.
:::

---

### Save It

```r
# Save sample metadata table for your project:
# row.names = FALSE drops the 1..12 row numbers.
write.csv(sample_info, "sample_metadata.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

---

### Step 5 — Merging

Table built. Table saved. One thing left: **attach it to `counts`.**

| | sample_id | cell_line | treatment | replicate |
|:--|:----------|:----------|:----------|:----------|
| `counts` column 1 says | `GSM3702795` | | | |
| `sample_info` row 1 says | `GSM3702795` | `PC9` | `Control` | `1` |

The two are lined up. The only thing missing is glue for the new label.

---

### 🔧 `paste()` — Gluing Text Together

```r
paste(..., sep = " ")
```

* **`...`** — anything you want joined; numbers are turned into text for you
* **`sep`** — what goes **between** them. The default is a single space.

The default is the part that bites:

```r
paste("PC9", "Control", 1)
# [1] "PC9 Control 1"

paste("PC9", "Control", 1, sep = "_")
# [1] "PC9_Control_1"
```

---

### 🔧 `paste()` on Whole Vectors

```r
paste(..., sep = " ")
```

And it works on whole vectors at once:

```r
paste(c("PC9", "PC9GR"), "Control", 1, sep = "_")
# [1] "PC9_Control" "PC9GR_Control"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 Always Set `sep` Explicitly
Spaces inside column names are a nuisance to type and easy to lose. Pick `_` and say so every time.
:::

---

### Now Use It — Name Your Columns

The table was worth building for this: relabel `counts` with it.

```r
colnames(counts) <- paste(sample_info$cell_line,
                          sample_info$treatment,
                          sample_info$replicate, sep = "_")

colnames(counts)
#  [1] "PC9_Control_1"    "PC9_Control_2"    "PC9_Control_3"    "PC9_Apatinib_1"
#  [5] "PC9_Apatinib_2"   "PC9_Apatinib_3"   "PC9GR_Control_1"  "PC9GR_Control_2"
#  [9] "PC9GR_Control_3"  "PC9GR_Apatinib_1" "PC9GR_Apatinib_2" "PC9GR_Apatinib_3"

# row.names = TRUE here — the gene IDs are row labels that mean something:
write.table(counts, "counts_sample_name_merge.tsv", sep = "\t", row.names = TRUE)

```

`head(counts)` now reads like an experiment, not a GEO accession list.

::: {.callout-note}
### ⚠️ This Works Because the Order Matches
`sample_info` row 1 was built from `colnames(counts)[1]`, so row *i* always describes column *i*. The GSM IDs are gone from `counts` — `sample_info$sample_id` is the only way back to GEO.
:::

## 📋 3. Vectorization & the apply Family

::: {.agenda data-section="3"}
:::
---

### The Problem

Each gene has 12 numbers — one per sample. We want **the average number per gene**.

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}

| gene | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| gene_1 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| gene_2 | 531 | 485 | 409 | 433 |
| gene_3 | 14 | 13 | 10 | 14 |
| ⋮ | ⋮ | ⋮ | ⋮ | ⋮ |
| gene_n | 43 | 41 | 50 | 60 |

:::

::: {.column width="8%"}

<div style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.6em; margin-top: 1.2em;">→</div>

:::

::: {.column width="32%"}

| mean |
|---:|
| **2.00** |
| **464.50** |
| **12.75** |
| ⋮ |
| **48.50** |

:::

:::::

---

### The Naive Way: a `for` Loop

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
# 3 genes x 4 samples
counts <- data.frame(
  gene = c("gene_1", "gene_2", "gene_3"),
  S1   = c(2, 531, 14),
  S2   = c(3, 485, 13),
  S3   = c(1, 409, 10),
  S4   = c(2, 433, 14)
)

means <- numeric(nrow(counts))

for (i in 1:nrow(counts)) {
  row <- counts[i, -1]                # pull out gene i's 4 numbers
  means[i] <- mean(as.numeric(row))   # a data frame row is not a vector
}

means
```

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {.callout-important}
### ⏱️ What If There Are More Samples? More Rows?
Every round pulls one row out of the table and averages it. More genes, more samples — more rounds, more copying.

**R will take forever!**
:::

:::

:::::

---

### apply(): The Margin Decides Everything

`apply()` does the same job as a loop, without the loop. It collapses your matrix along **one** axis, and works out the same statistic on each piece that is left.

Everything hinges on which axis — the **margin**.

---

### Margin 1: Mean of Each Row

Add each row across, divide by 4 (there are 4 samples):

```{webr-r}
#  gene_1:  (2 + 3 + 1 + 2) / 4 =  2.00
#  gene_2:  (531 + 485 + 409 + 433) / 4 = 464.50
#  gene_3:  (14 + 13 + 10 + 14) / 4 = 12.75
apply(counts[, -1], 1, mean) # [, -1] : drop the gene column - only the numbers
```

**3 rows in → 3 numbers out.**

---

### Margin 2: Mean of Each Column

Same table. Add each column down, divide by 3 (there are 3 genes):

```{webr-r}
#  S1:  (2 + 531 + 14)     / 3 = 182.33
#  S2:  (3 + 485 + 13)     / 3 = 167.00
#  S3:  (1 + 409 + 10)     / 3 = 140.00
#  S4:  (2 + 433 + 14)     / 3 = 149.67
apply(counts[, -1], 2, mean)
``` 

**4 columns in → 4 numbers out.**

---

### 📐 The Margin Is the Divisor

| | What you add up | Divide by | Answers |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---|
| `MARGIN = 1` | each **row**, across the columns | `ncol` = 4 | one per **row** → 3 |
| `MARGIN = 2` | each **column**, down the rows | `nrow` = 3 | one per **column** → 4 |

The margin decides **which axis survives**. Count the answers to check you got it right.

---

### apply() on the Real Matrix

MARGIN 1 does to the real matrix exactly what it did to the mock one:

```{r}
library(here)

counts <- read.delim(here("FCWT_2026", "lecture-06", "counts", "counts_annotated.tsv"))

# offset 2 columns (GeneID, Symbol) -> the 12 sample columns
mean <- apply(counts[, 3:ncol(counts)], 1, mean)
head(mean, 3)
# [1]   1.2500 512.8333  11.7500
```

---

### `rowMeans()` — The Shortcut

R ships a named version of that exact job:

```{r}
rowMeans(counts[, 3:ncol(counts)])
# 100287102    653635 102466751
#    1.2500 512.8333   11.7500
```

---

### 🕵️ When `apply()` Earns Its Place

Most common jobs already have a shortcut:

| Shortcut | Does the same job as |
|:---|:---|
| `rowMeans(x)` | `apply(x, 1, mean)` |
| `colMeans(x)` | `apply(x, 2, mean)` |
| `rowSums(x)` | `apply(x, 1, sum)` |

If a shortcut exists, use it — it is faster and easier to read.

Reach for `apply()` only when **no twin exists**: a statistic that is not row- or column-shaped, and where the margin genuinely changes what the number means.

---

### lapply() — A List, Every Time

One gene — the first row of `counts`:

```{webr-r}
reads <- counts[1, -1]     # gene_1's four reads
reads

# Run `sqrt()` on every element:
lapply(reads, sqrt)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The answer is **always** a list, whatever you put in. Each element keeps its name — `S1`, `S2`, `S3`, `S4` — so nothing is lost.
:::

---

### sapply() — The Same Work, Flattened

```{webr-r}
sapply(reads, sqrt)
#      S1       S2       S3       S4
# 1.414214 1.732051 1.000000 1.414214
```

Same numbers, no `$` prefixes — `sapply()` takes the list and tries to simplify it into a plain vector.

---

### tapply() — The Same Idea, With Labels

`lapply()` and `sapply()` walk a **list**. `tapply()` takes a **vector** plus the **labels that group it**:

```{webr-r}
reads <- c(2, 3, 1, 531, 485, 409)

# "gene_1", "gene_1", "gene_1", "gene_2", "gene_2", "gene_2"
gene  <- rep(c("gene_1", "gene_2"), each = 3)

tapply(reads, gene, mean)
```

Split the numbers into piles by `gene`, then run `mean` on each pile. The answer comes back **named after the groups** — the same 2.00 and 464.50 from the first slide.

---

### Which One Do You Want?

| | `lapply()` | `sapply()` | `tapply()`
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Returns | list, **always** | simplified vector, usually | vector per group
| Names kept? | yes | only if they survive simplification | yes 
| Surprises you? | never | sometimes returns a matrix | --- |

When the shape matters, use `lapply()`. When you just want the numbers and the shape is obvious, `sapply()` is fine.


---

### The Problem: 12 Numbers, 2 Answers Needed

MARGIN 2 gave us one mean per sample — **12 numbers**:

```{r}
# offset 2 columns (GeneID, Symbol) -> the 12 sample columns
sample_means <- colMeans(counts[, 3:ncol(counts)])
round(sample_means, 2)
#    PC9_Control_1 PC9_Control_2 PC9_Control_3  ... PC9GR_Apatinib_3
#             570.94         560.04         559.32   ...         494.85
```

But the question is not about samples. It is about **treatment**. We want two numbers: the mean of all Controls, and the mean of all Apatinibs.

How do you average numbers that carry labels?

---

### Step 1 — Get the Labels

```{r}
library(here)
counts_dir <- here("FCWT_2026", "lecture-06", "counts")

info <- read.csv(file.path(counts_dir, "sample_metadata.csv"))
info$treatment
#  [1] "Control"  "Control"  "Control"  "Apatinib" "Apatinib" "Apatinib"
#  [7] "Control"  "Control"  "Control"  "Apatinib" "Apatinib" "Apatinib"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🔑 `$` Pulls One Column
`info` is a table with four columns. `info$treatment` is just *"the `treatment` column"* — one vector of 12 labels, in the same order as `sample_means`.
:::

---

### Step 2 — Put Them Side by Side

Numbers on the left, labels on the right. Row *i* is the same sample in both:

```{r}
side_by_side <- data.frame(mean = round(sample_means, 2),
                           treatment = info$treatment)
```

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

| mean | treatment |
|---:|:---|
| 570.94 | Control |
| 560.04 | Control |
| 559.32 | Control |
| 554.25 | Apatinib |
| 559.01 | Apatinib |
| 524.23 | Apatinib |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

| mean | treatment |
|---:|:---|
| 544.62 | Control |
| 566.64 | Control |
| 569.34 | Control |
| 558.34 | Apatinib |
| 510.47 | Apatinib |
| 494.85 | Apatinib |

:::

:::::

---

### Step 3 — Average Each Pile

```{r}
tapply(sample_means, info$treatment, mean)
#  Apatinib   Control
#  533.5257  561.8162
```

That is all it did:

* `Control` = (570.94 + 560.04 + 559.32 + 544.62 + 566.64 + 569.34) / 6 = **561.82**
* `Apatinib` = (554.25 + 559.01 + 524.23 + 558.34 + 510.47 + 494.85) / 6 = **533.53**

---

### All Three Steps Together

Everything from the previous slides, start to finish:

```{r}
library(here)
counts_dir <- here("FCWT_2026", "lecture-06", "counts")

# --- the data -------------------------------------------------------
counts <- as.matrix(read.delim(file.path(counts_dir, "counts_sample_name_merge.tsv"),
                               row.names = 1))
info <- read.csv(file.path(counts_dir, "sample_metadata.csv"))

# --- Step 1: one mean per sample (12 numbers) ------------------------
sample_means <- apply(counts, 2, mean)

# --- Step 2: the matching label for each of those 12 -----------------
treatment <- info$treatment

# --- Step 3: average each pile (2 numbers) ---------------------------
tapply(sample_means, treatment, mean)
#  Apatinib   Control
#  533.5257  561.8162
```

---

### 💡 Why This Pattern Is Everywhere

**Group a numeric vector by a factor, summarise it.** That one line replaces most of your pivot tables.

Same numbers, a different grouping — one mean per **cell line**:

```{r}
tapply(sample_means, info$cell_line, mean)
#     PC9    PC9GR 
# 554.6308 540.7111 
```

::: {.callout-note}
### 🔍 Trivia
Differential expression has the same shape too — numbers grouped by a factor — but it needs a **count model** (DESeq2, edgeR), not a `tapply`.
:::

---

### Choosing the Right Tool

| Function | You give it | You get back |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `colMeans()` / `colSums()` | matrix | one mean or total per column |
| `rowMeans()` / `rowSums()` | matrix | one mean or total per row |
| `apply` | matrix / data frame + margin | vector or matrix |
| `lapply` | list / vector | list (always) |
| `sapply` | list / vector | simplified vector (usually) |
| `tapply` | vector + grouping factor | vector per group |
| `split` | vector + grouping factor | a list, one vector per group |

---

::: {.section-tag}
1. Vectorization & the apply Family · Exercise
:::

### ✍️ Exercise 3.1: Which Margin?

Rows are genes, columns are samples:

```{r}
m <- matrix(c(2, 3, 1, 2,
               531, 485, 409, 433,
               14, 13, 10, 14), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
#      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
# [1,]    2    3    1    2
# [2,]  531  485  409  433
# [3,]   14   13   10   14
```

You want **one mean per sample** — and the samples are the columns.

* a) `apply(m, 1, mean)`
* b) `apply(m, 2, mean)`
* c) `apply(m, 2, sum)`
* d) `rowMeans(m)`

---

::: {.section-tag}
3. Vectorization & the apply Family · Exercise
:::

### ✅ Exercise 3.1 — Solution

**b) `apply(m, 2, mean)`** — MARGIN 2 collapses down the rows, so the **columns survive**: one number per column.

| Option | Gives | Verdict |
|:---|:---|:---|
| a) `apply(m, 1, mean)` | `2  464.5  12.75` | wrong axis — one per **row** |
| b) `apply(m, 2, mean)` | `182.3  167  140  149.7` | ✅ one per **column** |
| c) `apply(m, 2, sum)` | `547  501  420  449` | right axis, wrong statistic |
| d) `rowMeans(m)` | `2  464.5  12.75` | one per **row** |

---

::: {.section-tag}
3. Vectorization & the apply Family · Exercise
:::

### ✍️ Exercise 3.2: What Does `lapply()` Give Back?

* a) a vector
* b) a list, always
* c) a matrix
* d) whatever the data happens to be

---

::: {.section-tag}
3. Vectorization & the apply Family · Exercise
:::

### ✅ Exercise 3.2 — Solution

**b) a list, always.** Whatever you feed it, `lapply()` comes back with a list — one element per input, names kept.

`sapply()` is the one that *tries* to simplify that list into a plain vector. Sometimes it succeeds, sometimes it hands you a matrix instead — which is exactly why `lapply()` is the safer default when the shape matters.

---

::: {.section-tag}
3. Vectorization & the apply Family · Exercise
:::

### ✍️ Exercise 3.3: Group and Summarise

12 numbers, each with a label:

```{r}
sample_means <- c(2, 3, 1, 2, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5)
treatment   <- rep(c("Control", "Apatinib"), each = 6)
```

You want the mean of the **Controls** and the mean of the **Apatinibs** — two numbers, not twelve.

* a) `tapply(sample_means, treatment, mean)`
* b) `apply(sample_means, treatment, mean)`
* c) `lapply(treatment, mean)`
* d) `mean(sample_means)`

---

::: {.section-tag}
3. Vectorization & the apply Family · Exercise
:::

### ✅ Exercise 3.3 — Solution

**a) `tapply(sample_means, treatment, mean)`** — split the numbers into piles by the labels, then average each pile. The result comes back named after the groups.

| Option | Gives | Verdict |
|:---|:---|:---|
| a) `tapply(...)` | `Control 3.17  Apatinib 2.67` | ✅ two numbers, named by group |
| b) `apply(...)` | **Error**: `dim(X) must have a positive length` | `apply()` wants a margin (1 or 2), not labels |
| c) `lapply(treatment, mean)` | `NA NA NA …` (×12) | it walks the **labels** — and you cannot average text |
| d) `mean(sample_means)` | `2.92` | one number for all 12 — the labels never used |

## 📋 4. Strings & Regular Expressions

::: {.agenda data-section="4"}
:::
---

### The Problem: Messy Gene Labels

Your gene list looks like this:

```{webr-r}
genes <- c("GAPDH", "ACTB-mouse", "CD8A-mouse", "IL6")
genes
```

You need the suffix stripped and the cases normalised — across 20,000 rows.

---

### grep(): Find the Matches

```{webr-r}
genes <- c("GAPDH", "ACTB-mouse", "CD8A-mouse", "IL6")

grep("mouse", genes)                  # which positions?
```

```{webr-r}
grep("mouse", genes, value = TRUE)    # which values?
```

```{webr-r}
grep("mouse", genes, invert = TRUE)   # which do NOT match?
```

::: {.callout-tip}
`grep()` gives you **indices**, so it plugs straight into subsetting: `genes[grep("mouse", genes)]`. Give it `value = TRUE` when you just want to eyeball the hits.
:::

---

### sub() vs gsub(): Replace Text

```{webr-r}
genes <- c("GAPDH", "HLA-DRB5-mouse", "CD8A-mouse", "IL6")

sub("-", "", genes)     # removes the FIRST hyphen only
```

```{webr-r}
gsub("-", "", genes)    # removes EVERY hyphen
```

::: {.callout-note}
`sub()` is the surgical tool, `gsub()` is the hammer. `gsub("-", "", x)` will strip **every** hyphen in a string — which is exactly why you should test on `genes` first, not on a production column.
:::

---

### Case, Length & Slicing

```{webr-r}
genes <- c("gapdh", "ACTB-mouse", "Cd8a-MOUSE", "il6 ")

toupper("gapdh")            # force case
```

```{webr-r}
nchar(genes)                # how many characters?
```

```{webr-r}
trimws("  Tumor  ")         # trim stray whitespace
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Whitespace is invisible and deadly. A label with one trailing space will never match a database key. Run `trimws()` on every text column you import.
:::

---

### Pattern Cheat Sheet

| Pattern | Matches | In gene labels |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `^` | start of string | `^mouse` |
| `$` | end of string | `mouse$` |
| `.` | any single character | `CD.8A` |
| `[A-Z]` | one character from a set | `[A-Z]+` |
| `+` | one or more | `mouse+` |
| `\\.` | a literal dot | `\\.1` |

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
genes <- c("HLA.1", "HLA1", "TP53", "HLA-A.1", "HLA.12", "HLA.1B", "mouse-HLA.1")
```

```{webr-r}
# A literal dot must be escaped: "\\.1$" = a real "." then "1" at the end
grep("\\.1$", genes, value = TRUE)
# [1] "HLA.1" "HLA-A.1" "mouse-HLA.1"
```

---

### ⚠️ The Dot Is a Wildcard

```{webr-r}
# Without the backslash, "." is a WILDCARD that matches any character
grep(".1$", genes, value = TRUE)
# [1] "HLA.1" "HLA1" "HLA-A.1" "mouse-HLA.1"
```

::: {.callout-warning}
### 🧬 Naming Changes Are Real Biology
HGNC renamed `MARCH1` and `SEPT1` to `MARCHF1` and `SEPTIN1` precisely because Excel kept mangling the old names. Never assume a symbol's current name — look it up.
:::

---

## 📋 5. Cleaning Missing Data (NA)

::: {.agenda data-section="5"}
:::
---

### Spot the Gap: is.na()

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
expression <- c(12, NA, 45, 0, NA, 99)
is.na(expression)
```

```{webr-r}
sum(is.na(expression))     # TRUE counts as 1
```

```{webr-r}
sum(!is.na(expression))
```

```{webr-r}
table(is.na(expression))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Always **count** the missing values per column before deciding what to do with them. `sum(is.na(x))` is the one line that tells you whether a dataset is trustworthy.
:::

---

### Why mean() Returns NA

```{webr-r}
expression <- c(12, NA, 45, 0, NA, 99)
mean(expression)                 # NA -> the whole answer is NA
```

```{webr-r}
mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE)   # na.rm = "NA remove"
```

::: {.callout-important}
### 🧬 Transcriptomic Connection
R propagates `NA` on purpose: **one unknown value makes the result unknown**. A single unmeasured spot must not silently become a zero. `na.rm = TRUE` is you explicitly accepting "drop the unknowns and compute on the rest".
:::

---

### Three Ways to Handle NA

```{webr-r}
expression <- c(12, NA, 45, 0, NA, 99)

expression[complete.cases(expression)]   # 1. drop the NAs
```

```{webr-r}
na.omit(expression)                       # 2. same thing, other name
```

```{webr-r}
mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE)            # 3. ignore them while computing
```

::: {.callout-note}
For a **vector**, 1 and 2 are identical. For a **data frame**, `na.omit(df)` deletes any row with an `NA` anywhere — which may delete far more than you intended.
:::

---

### Replace or Remove?

```{webr-r}
expression <- c(12, NA, 45, 0, NA, 99)
expression[is.na(expression)] <- 0   # replace with a baseline
expression

sum(c(0, 5, 12))   # a 0 count and a missing value are NOT the same thing
```

::: {.callout-important}
### ⚠️ Choosing Wisely
* **Remove** when the value was never measured and any guess would bias the result
* **Replace with 0** only when 0 is a biologically real state (an unexpressed gene)

In sequencing, "not detected" and "not present" are different claims. Say which one you mean.
:::

---

### 🧬 Practice: Clean a QC Table

```{webr-r}
qc <- data.frame(
  spot_id = c("S1", "S2", "S3", "S4"),
  umi     = c(1200, NA, 0, 640),
  mito    = c(4.1, 22.5, NA, 6.0)
)
```

::: {.slide-kicker}
Your Turn!
:::

Three steps — one at a time.

---

### ⚡ Step 1 — Add a `pass` column

`pass` is `TRUE` when `umi > 500`:

```{r}
qc$pass <- _______________
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
Compare a column with a number — you get a logical column back.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 1 — Add a `pass` column

```{r}
qc$pass <- qc$umi > 500
```

`TRUE  NA  FALSE  TRUE` — spot S2 has no `umi` value, so its `pass` is `NA` too.

---

### ⚡ Step 2 — Fill the gaps in a copy

In `qc_filled`, the missing `mito` values become `0`:

```{r}
qc_filled <- qc
qc_filled$mito <- ______________________________
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
`is.na(x)` finds the missing values, `ifelse(is.na(x), 0, x)` swaps them for something else.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 2 — Fill the gaps in a copy

```{r}
qc_filled <- qc
qc_filled$mito <- ifelse(is.na(qc_filled$mito), 0, qc_filled$mito)
```

`4.1  22.5  0  6.0` — `qc` itself is untouched.

---

### ⚡ Step 3 — Count the survivors

Spots that are fully measured **and** pass:

```{r}
keep <- ______________________________

sum(keep)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
`complete.cases(qc)` is one logical column, `qc$pass` is another. `&` joins them, `sum()` counts the `TRUE`s.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 3 — Count the survivors

```{r}
keep <- complete.cases(qc) & qc$pass

sum(keep)          # 2 spots survive
qc$pass            # TRUE  NA  FALSE  TRUE
qc_filled$mito     # 4.1  22.5  0  6.0
```

## 📋 6. Custom Functions

::: {.agenda data-section="6"}
:::
---

### Anatomy of a Function

A function is a **named recipe**: inputs, a body, and a returned value.

```{webr-r}
calc_percentage <- function(gene_count, total_umi) {
  pct <- (gene_count / total_umi) * 100
  return(pct)
}

# Call it
calc_percentage(25, 500)
```

::: {.callout-note}
`function(...)` defines the recipe, `calc_percentage(...)` runs it. Inputs you name in the definition are the **arguments**; the values you pass are the **arguments at the call**.
:::

---

### return() or the Last Line?

```{webr-r}
# Explicit is easier to read
median_count <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 0) {
    return(NA)
  }
  return(stats::median(x))
}

median_count(c(10, 40, 20))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Write `return()` when the function has more than a couple of steps. Your future self — and your reviewers — will thank you.
:::

---

### The Last Line Is the Return Value

```{webr-r}
# Without return(), R returns the last expression anyway
double_it <- function(x) {
  x * 2
}

double_it(21)
```

---

### Validate or Stop

```{webr-r}
calc_cpm <- function(gene_count, total_umi) {
  # Guard: refuse nonsense input immediately
  if (!is.numeric(gene_count) || !is.numeric(total_umi)) {
    stop("Counts must be numeric!")
  }
  if (total_umi <= 0) {
    stop("Library size must be greater than zero!")
  }

  return((gene_count / total_umi) * 1e6)
}

calc_cpm(450, 50000)
calc_cpm("450", 50000)
```

::: {.callout-important}
### 💡 `stop()` Is a Feature
A cryptic error ten lines later is expensive. A clear `stop()` at the door tells the analyst exactly what they passed in. This is **defensive programming** — write it today, thank yourself during review.
:::

---

### 🧬 Practice: Wrap Yesterday's CPM

```{webr-r}
# Yesterday we computed CPM by hand on two spots.
# Today: one function, any number of spots.
spots <- data.frame(
  spot_id = c("S1", "S2"),
  reads   = c(450, 200),
  total   = c(50000, 20000)
)
spots
```

::: {.slide-kicker}
Your Turn!
:::

Three steps — one at a time.

---

### ⚡ Step 1 — Write the function

`calc_cpm()` returns counts per million:

```{r}
calc_cpm <- function(reads, total) {
  if (any(total <= 0)) stop("Library size must be > 0")
  ____________________
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
CPM = reads divided by the library size, times one million.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 1 — Write the function

```{r}
calc_cpm <- function(reads, total) {
  if (any(total <= 0)) stop("Library size must be > 0")
  (reads / total) * 1e6
}
```

---

### ⚡ Step 2 — Add a `cpm` column

```{r}
spots$cpm <- ______________________________
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
Give your function both columns at once — R functions work on whole vectors.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 2 — Add a `cpm` column

```{r}
spots$cpm <- calc_cpm(spots$reads, spots$total)
```

`9000  10000` — one CPM per spot, no loop.

---

### ⚡ Step 3 — Add `mito_reads` and `mito_pct`

```{r}
spots$mito_reads <- c(12, 4)
spots$mito_pct  <- ______________________________
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 💡 Hint:
Mito percent = mito reads divided by all reads, times 100.
:::

---

### ✅ Step 3 — Add `mito_reads` and `mito_pct`

```{r}
spots$mito_reads <- c(12, 4)
spots$mito_pct  <- (spots$mito_reads / spots$reads) * 100

round(spots$cpm)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### 🎯 No Loop, No `sapply()`
`calc_cpm(spots$reads, spots$total)` gives **one CPM per spot** in a single line — R functions work on whole vectors. The guard needed `any()` so it still works when `total` is a vector.
:::

::: {.agenda data-section="7"}
:::
---

### ✍️ Exercise 1: Lists & Double Brackets

A QC report came back from the pipeline as a list:

```{webr-r}
qc_report <- list(
  sample_name = "Visium_HD_01",
  umi_counts  = c(200, 450, 12, 90, 800),
  pass_status = TRUE
)
```

::: {.slide-kicker}
Your Turn!
:::

1. Extract `umi_counts` **as a vector** (not wrapped in a list).
2. Compute the mean UMI count.
3. How many spots fall below `100` reads?

---

### ✅ Exercise 1: Lists & Double Brackets — Solution

```{webr-r}
qc_report <- list(
  sample_name = "Visium_HD_01",
  umi_counts  = c(200, 450, 12, 90, 800),
  pass_status = TRUE
)

# 1. [[ ]] unwraps the vector
counts <- qc_report[["umi_counts"]]

# 2. Mean library depth per spot
mean(counts)

# 3. How many low-quality spots?
sum(counts < 100)
counts[counts < 100]
```

::: {.callout-note}
`qc_report$umi_counts` would have worked too — `$` is shorthand for `[[` when the name is known. Use `[[ ]]` when the name comes from a variable.
:::

---

### ✍️ Exercise 2: apply() & Missing Data

A gene expression matrix arrived with holes in it:

```{webr-r}
test_data <- matrix(c(5, 10, NA, 2, 8, 12, 1, NA, 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
test_data
```

::: {.slide-kicker}
Your Turn!
:::

1. Replace every `NA` with `0`.
2. Compute the **median of each column** with `apply()`.
3. Print the column with the highest median.

---

### ✅ Exercise 2: apply() & Missing Data — Solution

```{webr-r}
test_data <- matrix(c(5, 10, NA, 2, 8, 12, 1, NA, 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 3)

# 1. Fill the holes
test_data[is.na(test_data)] <- 0

# 2. MARGIN 2 -> one median per column
col_medians <- apply(test_data, 2, median)
col_medians

# 3. Which column wins?
which.max(col_medians)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
`which.max()` and `which.min()` return **positions**, not values — the same idea as `grep()`. They are the standard way to find the top gene or the worst spot.
:::

---

### ✍️ Exercise 3: Clean the Gene List

```{webr-r}
genes <- c("gapdh", "ACTB-mouse", "Cd8a-MOUSE", "il6 ", "PECAM1-mouse")
```

::: {.slide-kicker}
Your Turn!
:::

1. Trim the whitespace and force everything to upper case.
2. Drop the `-mouse` suffix.
3. Report how many genes remain and print them.

---

### ✅ Exercise 3: Clean the Gene List — Solution

```{webr-r}
genes <- c("gapdh", "ACTB-mouse", "Cd8a-MOUSE", "il6 ", "PECAM1-mouse")

# 1. Whitespace + case
genes <- toupper(trimws(genes))

# 2. Strip the suffix
genes <- gsub("-MOUSE", "", genes)

# 3. Count and print
length(genes)
genes
```

::: {.callout-note}
Clean the **case first**, then the pattern — otherwise you need one regex per capitalisation. Order of operations matters in every cleaning pipeline.
:::

---

## 🧠 Recap in Seven Lines

* **Vectors** hold one type; **data frames** hold one type per column — count everything else you meet inside a list
* **`[[ ]]` unwraps** a list element, `[ ]` wraps it again
* **Vectors count from 1**, and a negative index removes
* **`grep()` finds, `sub()`/`gsub()` replace, `toupper()`/`trimws()` normalise**
* **`NA` propagates on purpose** — count it, then remove it or `na.rm = TRUE`
* **Vectorise, don't loop** — `colMeans()`, `apply(margin)`, `lapply`/`sapply`, `tapply`
* **Package logic into functions** and validate inputs with `stop()`
